name: Orange-Cinnamon
lede: Orange-Cinnamon is a warm, muted brown-orange whose compound name Robert Ridgway coined in 1912, pairing the fruit's color with the spice's.

sections.title: A spice-toned compound
sections.body:
The name pairs *orange* with *cinnamon*, the reddish-brown bark spice, in the same hyphenated style Ridgway used across his 1912 *Color Standards and Color Nomenclature*; this one sits on plate XXIX at hue 13 double-prime [1]. The ISCC-NBS committee filed the same Ridgway name into its 1955 dictionary, in block 53, the same block that holds [[light-orange]] [2].

The identical hex is also the closest match on file to *Ōdo-iro* (黄土色, literally "earthen yellow," i.e. ochre), a Japanese traditional color; again, the two names were coined independently, and the shared swatch is only a coincidence of measurement [1][3]. The nearest English look-alikes are [[antique-brass]], [[tawny]] and [[raw-sienna|Raw Sienna]], all close in hue [3].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: A close match appears in 936 of our 23,781 archived paintings, about 3.9 per cent, with the within-painting lens finding it in 605; more common than 84 per cent of our named colors [4]. It peaks in the 1500s at 1.9 times the archive's overall rate (113 paintings), and most often plays an accent [4]. Thomas Sully is its most devoted painter here, carrying it in 5 of his 26 archived works, and India is its most over-represented country, at 3 times the expected rate [4]. The earliest dated match, from the year 1000, sits 912 years before Ridgway's 1912 name, a floor, not a first sighting, as photographed, not a pigment test [4].
